newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai export growth may pick up - central banker.
newsitem.headline: Thai export growth may pick up - central banker.

text.p: A senior Bank of Thailand official said on Tuesday that growth in the country's exports could pick up in the latter half of this year after a sluggish first half.

Bandid Nijathavorn, head of the central bank's research department, told a group of business executives that despite the slowdown, the export growth target of 10.2 percent for the full year set by the bank in June might still be reached.
Thai exports grew only 3.8 percent during the first seven months of the year compared with 23.6 percent for the whole of 1995 and 21.3 percent in 1994.
"At the moment, we think that the central bank does not need to revise the economic forecast," he said.
Bandid said the economies of Thailand's major trading partners such as the United States and Japan were likely to improve during the second half of the year, and this should boost Thai exports.
Other factors included stable inflation, ample supply of agricultural products and various export-boosting measures recently introduced by the government, he added.

Bandid said the slowdown in the rate of export growth could exacerbate the current account deficit, which was 8.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995. The official forecast for 1996 is 7.8 percent of GDP.
"The current account deficit has not improved much so far. Although the imports decreased, the exports growth was also slower than expected," he said.
Bandid also urged the private sector to curb short-term foreign borrowing and rely more on local funding.
He said that although the country's short-term external debt was at a "manageable level," the central bank was concerned about the issue and would continue its effort to curb it.
Thailand's short-term debt was estimated at US$41.5 billion at the end of the first quarter of 1996.

Moody's Investors Service recently downgraded Thailand's short-term debt rating over concerns about an excessive build up of short-term debt and fears that any switch in sentiment towards Thailand could precipitate a balance of payments crisis.
